title: Probes and status page are auth-exempt; readiness body names deps, status page does not; no metric values on any public surface
context: The three public surfaces this blueprint contributes (liveness probe, readiness probe, public status page) have different audiences and therefore different acceptable leak surfaces. Orchestrators cannot hold service credentials, so probes must be auth-exempt. The readiness probe body is read by operators and integrations that already know the dependency set; naming deps in the probe response is functional. The status page is read by uncredentialed external readers; naming deps there is a leak. Getting the split wrong in either direction (auth-gate the probes, or leak internals to the public page) breaks the surfaces' function.
decision: The liveness path, the readiness path, and the status page path are declared at boot as auth-exempt in the application's authentication middleware. No cookie, no header, no source-IP allowlist gates access to those three paths. The readiness probe response body names each declared readiness dependency (state and checkedAt per dep); the public status page never names a readiness dependency, never renders internal identifiers (hostnames, replica ids, database identifiers, queue names, internal URLs, build hashes), and never renders raw metric values (request counts, latency numbers, error rates, queue depths). The status page vocabulary is the declared component list plus the declared notice fields; anything more granular belongs on an authenticated operator surface the project owns, not on the public page.
consequences: The public reader sees only what the operator has committed to as public contract; a security review of the public surface only inventories the declared component list and the declared notice fields. Operators who need the granular story fetch it from the readiness body (declared deps) or from project-authored authenticated dashboards. Auth-exempt is one-directional: an authenticated caller hitting a probe or the status page still gets the response (the exemption removes the gate, it does not gate against authenticated callers). A composing blueprint that wants the probes gated (e.g. a hardened-tier blueprint requiring source-IP allowlist on /readyz) authors a project-level auth policy that supersedes this ADR piecewise.

alternativesConsidered.name: Probes require a service token; the auth-exempt list is a v1.1 opt-in
alternativesConsidered.summary: The three surfaces are auth-gated by default; a project opts them out at deploy time if the orchestrator cannot hold credentials.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The default outcome would be projects that skip the opt-out step and ship gated probes the orchestrator cannot use, and gated status pages the intended readers cannot reach. The rcf-lite tier this blueprint targets does not have a security posture that justifies making unauth the opt-in shape.

alternativesConsidered.name: Public status page derives components from the readiness dependency set
alternativesConsidered.summary: The status page's component list is auto-generated from the readiness registry; no separate declaration.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Leaks the internal dependency vocabulary as public contract. Dependency names are chosen for operator clarity (payments-provider, sms-gateway); public component names are chosen for external reader clarity (Payments, Notifications). Merging the two surfaces the wrong names in the wrong audience.
